description: We are the team of six from Sarawak, bringing together 3 working professional and 3 university students with different experiences, perspectives and ideas. United by our curiosity about space, technology and innovation, we believe that solutions are built through collaboration and a willingness to learn.
summary: Forge FireWatch is a web app that turns MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data into one clear, day-by-day view of burning across the region you care about. It harmonizes both sensors, showing where they agree on the same event and where only one saw a signal, then layers maps, active-area summaries, persistence, attention scoring, peatland context, optional smoke drift hints, false-alarm filters, and CSV export for your own analysis. What ties it together for planners and responders is ground verification reporting. for each fire area you can submit an official-style field report (confirmed fire, false alarm, or not sure, with notes), see those verdicts alongside satellite evidence in the dashboard and downloads, and use them to prioritize where to look first and how to talk about risk with shared evidence, while final authority still rests with experts on the ground.
details:
What it is

  • Forge Firewatch, by team FORGEX6, is a web dashboard that helps people anywhere in the world understand satellite fire detections.
  • It uses MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data from NASA FIRMS, for the whole world, a chosen region, or any custom map area.

Satellite matching

  • MODIS and VIIRS detections that fall close together in place and time are matched.
  • Each detection is labelled Matched, MODIS-only or VIIRS-only.
  • When two satellites agree, a detection is more trustworthy.
  • A hotspot seen by only one satellite is shown clearly as less certain, not hidden.

Fire intelligence

  • Fire areas: nearby detections are grouped into one fire, showing how many days it has burned and which way it's spreading.
  • Location: each fire is labelled with the nearest city.
  • Peatland flag: marks fires on peat, a major source of long-lasting smoke and haze.
  • Attention score: combines satellite agreement, persistence, peatland and confidence, with a plain-language explanation.
  • Smoke outlook: uses the Open-Meteo wind forecast to list towns likely to be downwind of smoke in the next 24 hours.
  • Daily situation summary for the latest day.

Ground verification (key feature)

  • Firefighters, officials and members of the public can confirm a fire or mark it as a false alarm.
  • Enough confirmations raise a fire's attention level, and enough false-alarm reports lower it.
  • Locations reported as false alarms are flagged automatically in future data.
  • Known heat sources such as gas flares and factories are also flagged, along with FIRMS volcano, industrial and offshore detections in archive data.
  • Over time, this cuts the noise that wastes response effort.

Public awareness

  • Haze Patrol: a 60-second game with Asia, Europe and America scenarios that teaches young people how fires, peat, wind and haze are connected.

Benefits and impact

  • Faster and more confident decisions on which fires to check first.
  • Fewer wasted trips to false alarms.
  • Earlier smoke warnings for downwind communities.
  • More public awareness of how wildfires and peat fires affect health, schools and economies.

Tools

  • Python, Streamlit, pandas and Plotly.
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript (for the Haze Patrol game and the dashboard animations)
  • NASA FIRMS API (MODIS and VIIRS on S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21)
  • Open-Meteo API (wind forecast)
  • pytest and flake8, with GitHub Actions for automated testing.
  • AI tools (Cursor, Claude and Microsoft Copilot) helped build the prototype, and our team reviewed and tested everything they produced.

Creativity

  • Rather than treating every hotspot as a confirmed fire, we combine agreement between satellites, peatland context, wind direction and community reports.
  • Each fire gets an explained priority that people on the ground can adjust, instead of just a dot on a map.
  • A game reaches people that dashboards usually don't.

Factors we considered

  • Satellite detections are thermal anomalies, not proof of fire, so we're open about uncertainty.
  • MODIS and VIIRS differ in resolution and overpass timing.
  • Many false alarms come from industrial heat sources such as gas flares and factories.
  • Peatland drives long-lasting haze.
  • Times are shown in UTC so they're consistent worldwide.
  • The web app needs to be simple to open and use for non-experts.
  • It's clear about its limits, it supports official fire verification and air-quality monitoring but doesn't replace them.
